beats.on_screen: Title card: Low ferritin in teenage endurance athletes. Subtitle: Double-blind randomised controlled trial, SYN-C04.

beats.narration: Two hundred and fourteen athletes aged fifteen to eighteen, all with serum ferritin below thirty micrograms per litre, were randomised to either sixty milligrams of elemental iron as ferrous sulphate on alternate days, or a matched placebo, for twelve weeks. Alternate-day dosing was deliberate: it limits hepcidin-mediated blockade of absorption. Adherence, by pill count, was ninety-one percent.
beats.on_screen: Split diagram: 214 athletes, ferritin under 30 micrograms per litre, splitting into Iron 60 mg alternate days (n=107) and Placebo (n=107), over a 12-week bar. Callout: adherence 91%.

beats.narration: The primary endpoint was change in ferritin at twelve weeks. Ferritin rose by eighteen point four micrograms per litre on iron, against two point one on placebo. That is a between-group difference of sixteen point three micrograms per litre, with a confidence interval from twelve point nine to nineteen point seven, and a p-value below zero point zero zero one. Iron stores clearly refilled.
beats.on_screen: Bar chart, ferritin change in micrograms per litre: iron +18.4, placebo +2.1. Beneath it, difference 16.3, 95% CI 12.9 to 19.7, p < 0.001.

beats.narration: Haemoglobin barely moved. The between-group difference was one point five grams per litre, confidence interval zero point two to two point eight, which is small and imprecise. Gut side effects were more common on iron: twenty-one of one hundred and seven participants, versus nine of one hundred and seven on placebo.
beats.on_screen: Two panels. Left: haemoglobin difference 1.5 grams per litre, 95% CI 0.2 to 2.8. Right: GI adverse events, 21/107 iron versus 9/107 placebo.

beats.narration: Three limits matter for coaches. Everyone enrolled already had ferritin below thirty, so this says nothing about supplementing iron-replete athletes. No performance endpoint was measured at all, so faster or fitter is not a claim this trial can support. And it ran for twelve weeks only. Bottom line: alternate-day sixty milligram iron restores ferritin in adolescent athletes with low stores. Whether that translates into performance remains untested.
beats.on_screen: Checklist of three limitations, then closing card: Restores iron stores in deficient athletes. Performance effect: not measured.

final_narration:
Iron deficiency without anaemia is common in adolescent endurance athletes. This double-blind randomised controlled trial asked a narrow question: in young athletes whose iron stores are already low, does an alternate-day iron supplement actually refill those stores?
Two hundred and fourteen athletes aged fifteen to eighteen, all with serum ferritin below thirty micrograms per litre, were randomised to either sixty milligrams of elemental iron as ferrous sulphate on alternate days, or a matched placebo, for twelve weeks. Alternate-day dosing was deliberate: it limits hepcidin-mediated blockade of absorption. Adherence, by pill count, was ninety-one percent.
The primary endpoint was change in ferritin at twelve weeks. Ferritin rose by eighteen point four micrograms per litre on iron, against two point one on placebo. That is a between-group difference of sixteen point three micrograms per litre, with a confidence interval from twelve point nine to nineteen point seven, and a p-value below zero point zero zero one. Iron stores clearly refilled.
Haemoglobin barely moved. The between-group difference was one point five grams per litre, confidence interval zero point two to two point eight, which is small and imprecise. Gut side effects were more common on iron: twenty-one of one hundred and seven participants, versus nine of one hundred and seven on placebo.
Three limits matter for coaches. Everyone enrolled already had ferritin below thirty, so this says nothing about supplementing iron-replete athletes. No performance endpoint was measured at all, so faster or fitter is not a claim this trial can support. And it ran for twelve weeks only. Bottom line: alternate-day sixty milligram iron restores ferritin in adolescent athletes with low stores. Whether that translates into performance remains untested.
